title.back: Section review: Civics, Media & Everyday Economics
title.source: Section check: Civics, Media & Everyday Economics

intro.back: 10 questions about Lessons 20–24. No need to rush. You can look at the lessons again and try again as many times as you want.
intro.source: 10 questions about Lessons 20–24. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.0.question.back: Which one is a need, not a want?
questions.0.question.source: Which of these is a need, not a want?

questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Music videos are certainly fun, but you can live without them. So, it is a want. Look at Lesson 20 again.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Music videos are nice, but you can live without them. That makes them a want. Look back at Lesson 20.

questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A new football is certainly fun, but you can live without it. So, it is a want. Look at Lesson 20 again.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A new football is fun, but you can live without it. That makes it a want. Look back at Lesson 20.

questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. You must have clean water to live and stay healthy. So, it is a need.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. You must have clean water to live and stay healthy. That makes it a need.

questions.1.stimulus.title.note: Back-translation check: 'Pilihan rekaan' could be misread as 'design choice'. Check that 'rekaan' clearly means 'made-up' here. 'Contoh pilihan rekaan' is an option.

questions.1.stimulus.body.back: Amani and two of her friends share one tablet at a made-up learning centre. They have 30 more minutes to use it today. They can play a word game or watch a short science video. There is not enough time for both. They choose the science video.
questions.1.stimulus.body.source: Amani and two friends share one tablet at a made-up learning centre. They have 30 minutes left on it today. They can play a word game or watch a short science video. There is not enough time for both. They choose the science video.

questions.1.question.note: Translator: Source check: the key-terms table puts needs/wants and opportunity cost in Lesson 22 and resource in Lesson 20, but this quiz links Questions 1–2 to Lesson 20. Check which lesson numbers are right in the English. Back-translation check: The translator's source check still stands: the key-terms table puts needs/wants and opportunity cost in Lesson 22, but this check links Questions 1–2 to Lesson 20. Confirm the lesson numbers in the English. 'Kos lepas' is the standard term but is technical for young readers.
questions.1.question.back: What is the opportunity cost of their choice?
questions.1.question.source: What is the opportunity cost of their choice?

questions.1.options.0.text.back: The word game that is not played
questions.1.options.0.text.source: The word game they do not play

questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. The word game is the next best option that they give up. That is their opportunity cost.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The word game is the next-best thing they give up. That is their opportunity cost.

questions.1.options.1.text.back: The science video that they watch

questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The video is what they chose. Opportunity cost is what they give up. Look at Lesson 20 again.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The video is what they choose. The opportunity cost is what they give up. Look back at Lesson 20.

questions.1.options.2.text.back: The tablet that they share together
questions.1.options.2.text.source: The tablet that they all share

questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The tablet is the resource that they use. Opportunity cost is the thing that they give up. Look at Lesson 20 again.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The tablet is a resource they use. The opportunity cost is the thing they give up. Look back at Lesson 20.

questions.2.question.back: This is a made-up example. Jun repairs Lucia's broken chair. In return, Lucia teaches Jun a card game. No money is used. What is the name for an exchange like this?
questions.2.question.source: Here is a made-up example. Jun fixes a broken chair for Lucia. In return, Lucia teaches Jun a card game. No money is used. What is this kind of exchange called?

questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Scarcity means something is not enough for all uses. Here, two people exchange skills without money. Look at Lesson 21 again.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Scarcity means there is not enough for every use. Here, two people swap skills with no money. Look back at Lesson 21.

questions.2.options.1.text.note: Translator: This uses 'Sistem barter' as the glossary says. It is slightly longer than the wrong options. 'Barter' alone would also work if the length makes the answer easy to guess. Back-translation check: 'Sistem barter' follows the glossary, but it is longer than the wrong options and may give the answer away. Consider 'Barter' alone.

questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. A barter system means exchanging goods or skills without using money. Jun and Lucia exchange skills.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Barter means swapping a thing or a skill without using money. Jun and Lucia swap skills.

questions.2.options.2.text.note: Translator: 'Budget' is translated as 'belanjawan', which mainly means a money budget. 'Belanjawan masa' (Q5) may sound odd. 'Bajet' is a common everyday alternative. Use the same word as Lessons 21–22. Back-translation check: Use the same word for 'budget' as Lessons 21–22 (belanjawan or bajet). 'Belanjawan masa' (Q5) may sound odd to young readers.

questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A budget is a plan for money or time. Here, two people exchange skills without money. Look at Lesson 21 again.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A budget is a plan for money or time. Here, two people swap skills with no money. Look back at Lesson 21.

questions.3.question.back: Lesson 21 states that every exchange depends on trust. What happens when a seller cheats?
questions.3.question.source: Lesson 21 says every exchange depends on trust. What happens when a seller cheats?

questions.3.options.0.text.back: More people want to buy from him/her.
questions.3.options.0.text.source: More people want to buy from them.

questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. People do not want to buy from someone who cheats. Look at Lesson 21 again.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. People do not want to buy from someone who cheats. Look back at Lesson 21.

questions.3.options.1.text.back: People no longer trust that seller.

questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. If someone cheats, people no longer trust him/her. Then, trade becomes harder for everyone.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone.

questions.3.options.2.text.note: Back-translation check: Fixed: added 'pun' for 'at all', which had been dropped.
questions.3.options.2.text.source: Nothing changes at the market at all.

questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Cheating damages trust, and then trade becomes harder for everyone. Look at Lesson 21 again.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Cheating breaks trust, and then trade gets harder for everyone. Look back at Lesson 21.

questions.4.question.note: Back-translation check: 'Mei' is also the Malay word for May, so 'Belanjawan masa Mei' could be read as 'the time budget in May'. A native speaker should check whether to rephrase, for example 'Mei ada belanjawan masa: ...'.
questions.4.question.back: Mei's time budget has 15 minutes for reading English and 15 minutes for playing games on the shared phone. What does this show?
questions.4.question.source: Mei's time budget has 15 minutes for reading English and 15 minutes for games on the shared phone. What does this show?

questions.4.options.0.text.back: A budget can plan time, not only money.
questions.4.options.0.text.source: A budget can plan time, not only money.

questions.4.options.0.feedback.note: Translator: 'In the evening' is translated as 'pada waktu petang'. If the lesson means after dark, 'pada waktu malam' may fit better. Back-translation check: 'Pada waktu petang' can mean afternoon. If Lesson 22 means after dark, use 'pada waktu malam'.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. A budget is not only for money. Mei uses a budget to plan her time in the afternoon/evening.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Budgets are not only for money. Mei uses a budget to plan her time in the evening.

questions.4.options.1.text.back: A budget means Mei cannot play at all.
questions.4.options.1.text.source: A budget means Mei can never play games.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Mei still has 15 minutes to play. It's just that her time to play is shorter. Look at Lesson 22 again.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Mei still has 15 minutes for games. She just has less time for them. Look back at Lesson 22.

questions.4.options.2.text.back: A budget is only a plan for money.
questions.4.options.2.text.source: A budget is only ever a plan for money.

questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Mei's budget is a plan for her time. A budget is not only for money. Look at Lesson 22 again.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Mei's budget is a plan for her time. Budgets are not only for money. Look back at Lesson 22.

questions.5.question.back: Lesson 22 states that small short-term goals are useful. Why?
questions.5.question.source: Lesson 22 says that small, short goals are useful. Why?

questions.5.options.0.text.back: The goal does not need steps or a plan.
questions.5.options.0.text.source: They do not need any steps or plan.

questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. You still work towards a goal step by step. Look at Lesson 22 again.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. You still work towards a goal step by step. Look back at Lesson 22.

questions.5.options.1.text.back: The goal makes sure nothing will change.
questions.5.options.1.text.source: They make sure nothing will ever change.

questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Plans can still change. That is why small goals that you can work on now can help. Look at Lesson 22 again.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Plans can still change. That is why a small goal you can work on now helps. Look back at Lesson 22.

questions.5.options.2.text.back: You can start working on it now.
questions.5.options.2.text.source: You can start to work on them now.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Plans can change, but you can work on small goals now. One example is learning 10 new words a week.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Plans can change, but you can work on a small goal now. One example is learning 10 new words a week.

questions.6.stimulus.title.back: Message F, a made-up message from Lesson 23
questions.6.stimulus.title.source: Message F, a made-up message from Lesson 23

questions.6.stimulus.items.0.back: A picture of a fish that is as long as a bus.
questions.6.stimulus.items.0.source: A photo of a fish as long as a bus.

questions.6.stimulus.items.1.note: Back-translation check: 'Tulisannya berbunyi' reads a little oddly for a caption on a photo. Consider 'Kapsyennya berbunyi' or 'Tulisan pada gambar itu berbunyi'.
questions.6.stimulus.items.1.back: Its writing says: “Caught at Lakeside yesterday.”
questions.6.stimulus.items.1.source: The words say: “Caught at Lakeside yesterday.”

questions.6.stimulus.items.2.note: Translator: 'Edges of the fish' is translated as 'tepi badan ikan' (the outline of an edited image). Check that this reads naturally and matches Lesson 23. Back-translation check: Translator flag stands: check that 'tepi badan ikan' (signs of editing) reads naturally and matches Lesson 23. This also applies to option B (6.options.1.text).
questions.6.stimulus.items.2.back: The edges of the fish's body look strange.
questions.6.stimulus.items.2.source: The edges of the fish look strange.

questions.6.stimulus.items.3.back: No one else has a picture of this fish.
questions.6.stimulus.items.3.source: Nobody else has a photo of this fish.

questions.6.question.note: Back-translation check: Fixed: 'tidak benar' (not true) became 'tidak asli' (not genuine) to match 'asli/palsu' in the feedback. Check that it reads naturally.
questions.6.question.back: Which detail is a clue that the picture might not be true?
questions.6.question.source: Which detail is a clue that the photo may not be real?

questions.6.options.0.text.back: It is a picture, not a written message.
questions.6.options.0.text.source: It is a photo, not a written message.

questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A picture can be real or already changed. Just because it is a picture does not mean it is fake. Look at Lesson 23 again.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A photo can be real or changed. Being a photo does not show it is fake. Look back at Lesson 23.

questions.6.options.1.text.back: The edges of the fish's body look strange.
questions.6.options.1.text.source: The edges of the fish look strange.

questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Edges that look strange can show that the picture has been changed with an app. Besides, no one else has a picture of this fish.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Strange edges can show that a photo was changed with an app. Also, nobody else has a photo of this fish.

questions.6.options.2.text.back: It mentions the place where the fish was caught.
questions.6.options.2.text.source: It says where the fish was caught.

questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Mentioning a place name does not show that the picture is fake. Think about how the fish itself looks. Look at Lesson 23 again.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Naming a place does not show a photo is fake. Think about how the fish itself looks. Look back at Lesson 23.

questions.7.stimulus.body.note: Translator: 'City Park' and 'Lakeside' (Q7) are kept as made-up place names. Check that they match how Lesson 23 handles them. Back-translation check: Translator flag stands: check that 'City Park' and 'Lakeside' are kept as in Lesson 23. 'Ternampak' suggests she saw it by chance. 'Nampak' would be more neutral.
questions.7.stimulus.body.back: Pia plays in a football team. She happens to see a message in a group chat. The message says: “Our match at City Park is now on Sunday. Tell the whole team.” The message has no name and no date. Pia does not know who wrote it.
questions.7.stimulus.body.source: Pia plays in a football team. She sees a message in a group chat. It says: “Our match at City Park is now on Sunday. Tell the whole team.” The message has no name and no date. Pia does not know who wrote it.

questions.7.question.back: What is the best thing for Pia to do first?
questions.7.question.source: What is the best thing for Pia to do first?

questions.7.options.0.text.back: Send to the whole team right now
questions.7.options.0.text.source: Send it to the whole team right now

questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The message has no name or date, so Pia cannot trust it yet. It is safer to check it first. Look at Lesson 23 again.
questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The message has no name or date, so Pia cannot trust it yet. It is safer to check first. Look back at Lesson 23.

questions.7.options.1.text.back: Believe it, because it sounds very confident
questions.7.options.1.text.source: Believe it, because it sounds very sure

questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A message can sound confident but still not be true. Pia needs to check it first. Look at Lesson 23 again.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A message can sound sure and still be wrong. Pia needs to check it first. Look back at Lesson 23.

questions.7.options.2.text.back: Ask her coach whether the message is true
questions.7.options.2.text.source: Ask her coach if the message is true

questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Her coach is a source that can be trusted. Pia can confirm the message before sharing it.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Her coach is a trusted source. Pia can verify the message before she shares it.

questions.8.question.note: Back-translation check: 'Pihak berkepentingan' is the glossary term but sounds formal for young readers.
questions.8.question.back: Lesson 24 states that bus users are stakeholders. What does that word mean?
questions.8.question.source: Lesson 24 says the bus users are stakeholders. What does that word mean?

questions.8.options.0.text.note: Back-translation check: Fixed: 'terkesan' became 'terjejas', the usual Malaysian word for 'affected' ('terkesan' leans Indonesian or means 'moved/impressed'). The same fix was made in 8.1 and 8.2 feedback. 'Terjejas' sounds a little negative. Check that it suits 'a plan affects' too.
questions.8.options.0.text.back: People or groups who are affected by a problem
questions.8.options.0.text.source: A person or group that a problem affects

questions.8.options.0.feedback.note: Back-translation check: 'Pengurus pusat' (centre manager) could be read as 'central manager'. Match Lesson 24's wording, for example 'pengurus pusat pembelajaran' if that is the centre meant.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. Rubbish at the bus stop affects bus users and the centre manager. So, they are stakeholders.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The litter at the bus stop affects the bus users and the centre manager. So they are stakeholders.

questions.8.options.1.text.back: People who sell goods at market stalls
questions.8.options.1.text.source: A person who sells goods at a market stall

questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Bus users do not sell anything. Stakeholders are people who are affected by a problem or plan. Look at Lesson 24 again.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The bus users are not selling anything. A stakeholder is someone a problem or plan affects. Look back at Lesson 24.

questions.8.options.2.text.back: People who check whether messages are true
questions.8.options.2.text.source: A person who checks if a message is true

questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Checking messages is part of Lesson 23. Stakeholders are people who are affected by a problem or plan. Look at Lesson 24 again.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Checking messages is part of Lesson 23. A stakeholder is someone a problem or plan affects. Look back at Lesson 24.

questions.9.question.back: What does Lesson 24 say about ways to help the community?
questions.9.question.source: What does Lesson 24 say about ways to help a community?

questions.9.options.0.text.note: Back-translation check: Fixed: 'setiap hari' (every day) became 'harian' to keep 'everyday' (ordinary) and match 'tindakan harian' in 9.1 feedback. A native speaker should confirm.
questions.9.options.0.text.back: Small actions every day can bring change.
questions.9.options.0.text.source: Small, everyday actions can make a difference.

questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. Reading with younger children or keeping a shared room clean can help the community.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Reading with a younger child or keeping a shared room clean can help a community.

questions.9.options.1.text.back: Only big campaigns can bring real change.
questions.9.options.1.text.source: Only big campaigns can make a real difference.

questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Helping does not necessarily mean big campaigns. Daily actions are also important. Look at Lesson 24 again.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Helping does not have to mean a big campaign. Everyday actions matter too. Look back at Lesson 24.

questions.9.options.2.text.note: Back-translation check: Fixed: the earlier version dropped 'at all'. The new version says 'you can only help if you speak in public'. Check that it reads naturally.
questions.9.options.2.text.back: You must speak in front of a crowd to help.
questions.9.options.2.text.source: You must speak in public to help at all.

questions.9.options.2.feedback.note: Back-translation check: Fixed word order: 'tidak perlu sama sekali' became 'langsung tidak perlu'. Check that it reads naturally.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. You do not need at all to speak in front of a crowd, post something online or take risks in order to help. Look at Lesson 24 again.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to help. Look back at Lesson 24.

results.high.back: Well done. You know a lot about making choices, checking messages and helping the community.
results.high.source: Well done. You know a lot about making choices, checking messages and helping a community.

results.middle.back: Good. You answered many questions correctly. Look at the lessons again for the questions you missed, and try again if you want.
results.middle.source: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.

results.low.back: Thank you for trying. Look at Lessons 20–24 again, then try again. You can take as much time as you need.
results.low.source: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 20–24, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
